food.text: Nikolaos Tselementes was a Greek chef whose surname became a Greek synonym for "cookbook". After returning to Greece in 1932, he brought out the first complete cookbook in Greek, which had over fifteen official reprints in the following decades.

In the 20th century, French cuisine influenced Greek cooking largely through the French-trained chef Nikolaos Tselementes. Greek cuisine itself is founded on the triad of wheat, olive oil, and wine, and continues traditions from Ancient Greek and Byzantine cooking.

Balkan cuisine combines characteristics of European cuisine with some from West Asia. Except for Slovenian cuisine, these cuisines have a notable Turkish influence due to Ottoman occupation, and Ottoman cuisine remains the historical foundation of modern Balkan cooking.

Ottoman culinary influence survived the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire. Albanian, Greek, Romanian, Serbian, Bulgarian, Macedonian and Bosnian cuisine all share in the heritage of Ottoman culinary culture.

Tselementes studied cooking for a year in Vienna and then worked for various embassies in Greece. In 1919 he became manager of the hotel "Hermes", and the next year he left for America, where he worked in well-known restaurants and studied cooking, confectionery and dietetics.
Thanks to Tselementes, Greek housewives learned of béchamel sauce, pirozhki, and bouillabaisse. He also created the modern versions of mousaka, pastitsio, and anginares (artichokes) alla polita.
Tselementes created the modern Greek version of moussaka by combining an existing eggplant dish with a French-style gratin topping. He is also credited with creating the modern Greek pastitsio.

Tselementes began publishing the magazine Cooking Guide (Odigos Mageirikis) in 1910. It included recipes as well as nutritional advice, international cuisine and cooking news. In 1950 he published his only book in English, Greek Cookery.

Pontic Greek cuisine, from the southern shore of the Black Sea, includes a nettle soup called kinteata, shared with Iranian cuisine. Pontians also had their own variety of borscht, which they called portz.

Pontic Greeks ate a fried-egg dish called foustoron, prepared differently by region. Pontians in coastal Sourmena ate chapsofoustoron, an omelette with anchovies, while around Ordu they ate melofoustoron, a honey omelette.
Kollyva is a sweet dish of boiled grains, nuts, raisins, and sugar in Pontic Greek cuisine. It is traditionally eaten at funerals and memorial services.

art.text: At the start of the 20th century, landscape painting held sway in Greece, and painters turned to the study of light and color. The pull of Munich weakened, and Paris became the main attraction for Greek artists of the period.

Athens's National Gallery reopened on 24 March 2021 after an 8 year refurbishment, a day before the 200th anniversary of the Greek War of Independence. It had been closed since March 2013 because of expansion works.

Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, won wide recognition in France in the early 20th century. He gained lifelong membership of the Académie française after a critic praised him as an artist capable of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto.

Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions of both painting and poetry. In the late 1960s, Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism.

Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of Greek art in the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas. Their later development led them down other roads, but always within the avant-garde movement, with a Greek dimension.

After World War II, work began on a new building for Athens's National Gallery. The sculptures were relocated to the new National Glyptotheque, and a new wing for the main building was finally completed in 2021.

In 2025, an exhibition at the National Gallery in Athens titled "The Allure of the Bizarre" was attacked by Niki MP Nikolaos Papadopoulos and a companion. They threw four paintings to the floor and broke their glass frames, saying the works were offensive to Orthodox Christianity, and were briefly detained.

war.text: The Greek Civil War lasted from 1946 to 1949 and began soon after World War II ended. Communist-led rebels declared a people's republic, the Provisional Democratic Government of Greece, and were supported by Albania and Yugoslavia. With British and American support, the royal government forces prevailed. The war was noted for the scale of war crimes committed by both factions, including massacres and child abductions, and for its high casualty rate: at least 80,000 people died.

On 28 October 1940, Mussolini issued an ultimatum demanding Greek territory, and Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas rejected it. The Italian invasion from Albania penetrated only a few kilometers into Greece. Italian forces met unexpectedly tenacious resistance from the Hellenic Army and struggled with the mountainous, muddy terrain.

The Axis occupation of Greece began in April 1941 with the German invasion, and after the Battle of Crete the occupation ran from June 1941. It destroyed 80% of Greek industry, 90% of its bridges and 25% of its forests, and an estimated 7–11% of the civilian population died as a result. In Athens 40,000 civilians died of starvation (300,000 in the whole country), and tens of thousands more died in reprisals by Nazis and their collaborators. Germany and Bulgaria withdrew from the mainland in early October 1944, while German garrisons on Crete and some Aegean islands surrendered only in May and June 1945.

Greece stayed neutral when World War I broke out in August 1914. King Constantine favoured neutrality, while Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos was pro-Allied. Their disagreement led to the National Schism, which split the state between two rival governments, until Greece joined the Allies in the summer of 1917.

On 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo, Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a grenade at the car of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and injured two of his aides. An hour later Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, found the car in a street after it took a wrong turn and fired two pistol shots, fatally wounding Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on 28 July, and the Russian Empire mobilised in Serbia's defence. In Bosnia, Austro-Hungarian authorities imprisoned about 5,500 prominent Serbs, 700 to 2,200 of whom died in prison, and sentenced a further 460 to death.

The Macedonian front stayed mostly stable through World War I, and both sides settled into relatively static trench warfare across a 350 km wide front. On 30 May 1918, Greek forces attacked the Bulgarians and defeated them at the Battle of Skra-di-Legen. In September, Allied forces under French general Louis Franchet d'Espèrey broke through the German, Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian lines. The Greek military suffered an estimated 5,000 deaths from the nine divisions that took part in the war, and total casualties exceeded 24,000 men.

After the 4th of August Regime came to power in 1936 under Ioannis Metaxas, plans were laid to reorganise the Greek armed forces. They included building the Metaxas Line, a defensive fortification along the Greco-Bulgarian frontier.

The Democratic Army of Greece moved to conventional warfare in 1947 and won military victories, but in December 1947 some 1,200 of its fighters were killed in the Battle of Konitsa. It was defeated in the final stages by the Hellenic Army under Marshal Alexandros Papagos. In summer 1948 the DSE's III Division in the Peloponnese, with 20,000 fighters, was doomed for lack of ammunition; most of them, including the commander Vangelis Rogakos, were killed in battle with nearly 80,000 National Army troops. To terrify urban areas that had helped the division, government-side forces decapitated a number of dead fighters and placed the heads in central squares.

On 13 December 1943, Wehrmacht troops of the 117th Jäger Division carried out the extermination of the entire male population of Kalavryta and then totally destroyed the town. It is one of the most infamous massacres of the German occupation zone. It was one of a series of reprisals in which the Germans executed some 21,000 Greeks, among them the 317 inhabitants of Kommeno, shot and the village torched, and 218 civilians killed at Distomo.

Before the war, Italy ran a hostile press campaign against Greece, accusing it of being a British ally. A number of provocations culminated in the Italian sinking of the Greek light cruiser Elli on 15 August. Mussolini's ultimatum followed on 28 October.

After the Civil War, DSE or ELAS fighters and suspected sympathizers were often persecuted, imprisoned and exiled, most prominently on prison islands such as Gyaros and Makronisos. Captured communist leaders were sentenced to death, and almost 100,000 ELAS fighters and communist sympathizers serving in DSE ranks were imprisoned, exiled or executed. Thousands languished in prison for many years. Purges and internments peaked during the military dictatorship of 1967 to 1974.

After Italy occupied Albania in spring 1939, the Greek General Staff prepared the "IB" (Italy-Bulgaria) plan, anticipating a combined offensive by both countries. Because of the alliance's overwhelming superiority in manpower and matériel, the plan was purely defensive. It prescribed a gradual retreat of Greek forces in Epirus to gain time for mobilization.

literature.text: Téa Obreht won the 2011 Orange Prize for Fiction for her debut novel The Tiger's Wife. At age 25 she became the youngest winner of the prize to date. The novel was also a finalist for the National Book Award for Fiction and the Dylan Thomas Prize.

The Tiger's Wife is set in an unnamed Balkan country, from the mid 20th century to the early 21st. A young doctor hears her grandfather's stories about a "deathless man" who never dies, and about a deaf-mute girl who befriends a tiger escaped from a nearby zoo.

In 1994, Alice Munro's short story "The Albanian Virgin" was first published in The New Yorker. In it, a Canadian woman held hostage by Albanians takes the vow of a sworn virgin to avoid forced marriage. The tradition lets women live socially recognized as men.

The poet Charles Simic called The Tiger's Wife "a remarkable first novel" in The New York Review of Books. He said it mixes different kinds of narrative in a way that recalls Mikhail Bulgakov, Gabriel García Márquez, and Milorad Pavić, the Serbian author of Dictionary of the Khazars.

Miltos Sachtouris belongs to the second wave of Greek Surrealism. His books include The Forgotten (1945), The Walk (1960), and Vessel (1971). His poetry is described as simultaneously compassionate and macabre.

Poet and art historian Eleni Vakalo has been described as "one of the most respectable figures of post-war intellectual life". She incorporated elements of Surrealism and is known for Theme and Variations (1945), Recollections from a Nightmarish City (1948), and Genealogy (1972).

Nanos Valaoritis, like Sachtouris, belongs to the second wave of Greek Surrealism. In works such as The Punishment of the Magi (1947) and Breeding Ground for Germs (1977), he frequently restored older forms. He used surrealistic modes to achieve poetic self-transcendence.

The Tiger's Wife was largely written while Téa Obreht attended Cornell University. Portions were excerpted in The New Yorker in June 2009. She summarized it as a family saga in a fictionalized Balkan province, about doctors and their relationships to death through the region's wars.

Greece's '70s Generation of poets included Katerina Gogou, with Three Clicks Left (1978) and Idionymo (1980). Others were Manolis Pratikakis, Argyris Chionis, Yannis Kondos, Michalis Ganas and Maria Laina. Antonis Fostieris published The Great Trip in 1971 and Precious Oblivion in 2003.

The Orange Prize, which Téa Obreht won, recognized "excellence, originality and accessibility in women's writing from throughout the world". At the time it included £30,000 in cash and the "Bessie", a limited edition bronze figurine.

Greek books from the '80s and '90s include History (1982) by Giorgis Giatromanolakis and The Crowd (1985-1986) by Andreas Franghias. Also notable are Pavlos Matesis's The Daughter (1990) and Nikos Themelis's The Search (1998), and Lenos Christidis published The Slapfish in 1997.

politics.text: In the First Balkan War, which began on 8 October 1912, Greece, Serbia, Montenegro and Bulgaria attacked the Ottoman Empire as the Balkan League. They stripped it of its European provinces, leaving only Eastern Thrace under Ottoman control. The victory set the stage for the July crisis of 1914.

Italy invaded Greece from Albania on 28 October 1940, starting the Greco-Italian War. The Greek Army pushed the Italians back into Albania, delivering the first major Axis setback of the war. Greek successes forced Nazi Germany to intervene.
politics.source_title: Military history of Greece during World War II

politics.text: Greece has been a member of the European Union since 1981. Slovenia joined in 2004, Bulgaria and Romania in 2007, and Croatia in 2013. Other Balkan states have said they hope to join at some future date.

After the dissolution of Yugoslavia, six states achieved internationally recognized sovereignty: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Serbia. In 2008, while under UN administration, Kosovo declared independence. In July 2010, the International Court of Justice ruled that the declaration was legal.

The Second Balkan War began on 16 June 1913, when Bulgaria, dissatisfied with its share of Macedonia, attacked its former allies. Serbian and Greek armies repelled the offensive and invaded Bulgaria, while Romania struck from the north. Civilians suffered badly: the Greek army plundered and burnt the mostly Bulgarian town of Kilkis and massacred part of its population, and about 160 Bulgarian villages were destroyed with most of their people expelled. The Bulgarian army in retaliation destroyed Nigrita, Serres and Doxato and massacred non-combatant Greek inhabitants at Sidirokastro and Doxato. In the Treaty of Bucharest, Bulgaria was forced to cede the southern part of Dobruja to Romania.

The Greek genocide was the systematic killing of the indigenous Christian Ottoman Greek population of Anatolia because of their religion and ethnicity, carried out between 1912 and 1923. It included massacres, summary executions, and forced deportations on death marches through the Syrian Desert. Several hundred thousand Ottoman Greeks died, either murdered outright or as intentional victims of hunger, disease, and exposure. Most refugees and survivors fled to Greece, adding over a quarter to its prior population, and those who remained were transferred under the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey.

The Pontic Greek genocide began in 1914 under the Committee of Union and Progress regime, led by the Three Pashas, and after a pause in 1918 to 1919 continued into 1923 under the Kemalist regime. Greek men aged 18 to 48 were conscripted into labor battalions and worked to death, sometimes more than 90 percent of them dying, while women, children and the old were marched in deportation caravans with death rates of 80 to 90 percent, many freezing, starving or being killed by their escorts, and villages were burned, with some people burned alive. About 353,000 Pontic Greeks were killed and 1.5 million expelled, approximately half of the pre-genocide Pontic population dying.

Greece was occupied and divided between Germany, Italy and Bulgaria, while the King and government fled into exile in Egypt. Resistance began again in 1942 and grew enormously in 1943 and 1944, and German mass reprisals against civilians brought massacres such as those at Kommeno, Distomo and Kalavryta. Greece suffered at least 250,000 dead during the Axis occupation, and the country's Jewish community was almost completely exterminated in the Holocaust; the Greek government's report claims 600,000 died of hunger and related diseases, and 69,151 Greek Jews were deported, of whom only 2,000 returned. Mainland Greece was liberated in October 1944, and by 1946 a civil war erupted that lasted until 1949.

politics.text: Greek prime minister Metaxas defied an Italian demand for surrender on 28 October 1940, starting the Greco-Italian War. After seven months of hard fighting the Italians lost nearly one third of Albania. Germany then intervened to save its ally and invaded Yugoslavia in 1941.

After Slobodan Milošević, elected Serbian president between 1989 and 2000, was overthrown, he was handed over for trial to the International Criminal Tribunal. He faced charges for crimes against international humanitarian law during the Yugoslav wars. He died of a heart attack in 2006 before a verdict could be released.

Some Greek Communist refugees fled after the 1946 to 1949 Greek Civil War, mainly from Greek Macedonia and northern Greece. They settled in the USSR, Czechoslovakia and other Eastern Bloc states. Many of those who settled in Ukraine were in fact Pontic Greeks or Caucasus Greeks.

philosophy.text: Hellenism, also called Hellenic Polytheism, is a modern neopagan religion based on ancient Greek religion. Its followers worship the Greek gods through prayer, offerings, household and public rituals, and annual festivals. It emphasizes values such as Eusebeia (piety), Arete (virtue), and Xenia (hospitality).

Eastern Orthodoxy is recognised in the Greek Constitution as the "prevailing" faith of the country, though the Constitution also guarantees freedom of religious belief for all. In 2022, Orthodoxy represented 81 to 90% of the population of Greece.

Greece has seen a gradual rise in people identifying as atheist, agnostic, or non-religious. In 2024, 27% of Greeks reported being indifferent to religion, up from 18% in 2018. Religion is still a key part of identity for most Greeks, and 76% said in a 2015 to 2017 survey that their nationality is defined by Christianity.

Stathis Psillos, a Greek philosopher of science, is Professor of Philosophy of Science and Metaphysics at the University of Athens. In 2015 he was classified among the 91 most cited living philosophers with public Google Scholar pages.
Psillos was among the founders of the European Philosophy of Science Association. He served as its first elected President, from 2007 to 2009.
In October 2011, in the midst of the Greek socio-economic crisis, Psillos organised the 3rd congress of the European Philosophy of Science Association. It was held in Athens.

The modern revival of Hellenism began in the 20th century, with organized movements emerging in Greece during the 1990s. Many practitioners describe it as the continuation of an enduring tradition, but most historians regard it as a modern reconstruction of ancient Greek religion.

In May 2006 an Athens court granted official recognition to the veneration of the Ancient Greek pantheon. In 2017, Hellenism was legally recognized as a "known religion" in Greece, which let it establish places of worship and let its clergy officiate at marriages.

A 2024 survey by Metron Analysis for To Vima found that 66% of Greeks declared that they have a religion, but only 15% reported attending church regularly. This suggests a partial retreat from religious practice in a country long known for the strong presence of the Greek Orthodox Church.

The Atheist Union of Greece was founded in 2010 and legally recognized in 2012. It promotes secularism and the separation of church and state, operates independently of political parties and religious ideologies, and is governed by an elected five-member secretariat.

Psillos began by studying physics at the University of Patras. A state scholarship then took him to King's College London for an MSc in History and Philosophy of Science, and in 1994 he earned a PhD there under David Papineau.

On 22 January 2007, the Hellenist group Ellinais held a ceremony at the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens. It was the first such rite at the temple since the ancient Greek religion was outlawed by the Roman government in the late 4th century. Participants dressed as ancient warriors left their swords and spears outside the site.

In 2019, Greece's Council of State ruled that including students' religious affiliation on graduation certificates and other school documents was unconstitutional. The Atheist Union of Greece had challenged the recording of religion on school diplomas and advocated for exemptions from religious education.
His 1994 doctoral thesis was titled Science and Realism: A Naturalistic Investigation into Scientific Enquiry. Its examiners were John Worrall and William Newton-Smith.

Father Eustathios Kollas, who presided over a community of Greek Orthodox priests, responded to the 2007 Ellinais ceremony with harsh words. He called the participants "a handful of miserable resuscitators of a degenerate dead religion." The BBC had referred to the event as a show of "intentional publicity".

Despite the 2006 court ruling, the Greek Ministry of Culture and Sports continued to disallow ceremonies of any kind at archaeological sites. In August 2008, Ellinais adherents gathered at the Acropolis to give libations and offerings to the goddess Athena. They also protested the removal of architectural pieces from the temples to a new museum.

The Routledge Companion to the Philosophy of Science, which Psillos edited with Martin Curd, was named a Choice Outstanding Academic Title for 2008. A second revised and expanded edition followed in 2013.
tags: The Routledge Companion to the Philosophy of Science

philosophy.text: Between 1993 and 1998 Psillos was assistant editor and then deputy editor of the British Journal for the Philosophy of Science. From 2009 to 2014 he edited the journal Metascience, and in 2015 he was elected to Academia Europaea.
tags: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science

culture.text: The 1950s and early 1960s are considered by many the Golden age of Greek cinema. More than sixty films per year were made, with the majority having film noir elements. Directors and actors such as Michael Cacoyannis, Melina Mercouri and Irene Papas became important figures in Greece.

Most Pontian Greeks were displaced in the early 20th century after the Greek genocide and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. Some dances were lost because the people who practiced them were killed during the Greek genocide. Most Pontians today live in the diaspora, where folk dances such as the serra and instruments such as the Pontic lyra remain important to their communities.

Cacoyannis directed Stella in 1955, written by Kampanellis, and later directed Zorba the Greek with Anthony Quinn. Zorba the Greek received nominations for Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Film.
Theo Angelopoulos directed a series of notable films during the 1970s and 1980s. His film Eternity and a Day won the Palme d'Or and the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury at the 1998 Cannes Film Festival.

Romeika, the Pontic Greek language, is endangered. Ethnologue counted 778,000 speakers in 2015, about 400,000 of them in Greece. Traditionally it was spoken at home, while standard Greek was used in schools, churches and written records, so little was ever written in Romeika. Pontian children growing up in Greece in the mid-20th century report being beaten for speaking Romeika in schools.

The Greek publisher Αρχειον Ποντου (Pontic Archive) has published texts in Romeika since 1928. Apolas Lermi, a singer and guitarist from Trapezounta, released the Romeika-language albums "Kalandar" in 2011 and "Romeika" in 2016.
Pontian theatre troupes exist in Athens and throughout northern Greece to perform Pontian plays. The first of these troupes was founded in 1949.

In 2019, Merve Tanrıkulu, a Turkish singer from Trapezounta, released an original Romeika-language song called Romeika ninni, meaning "Romeika lullaby". Giannis Vasiliadis, who comes from a Soviet Greek family, wrote the song "Kavkaz" in Romeika.
